svg.text: Cache flush — DCR read to last writeback drained
One flush primitive exists: whole-cache invalidate-and-writeback. It is triggered by a DCR READ, carried as an ordinary MemReq with attr.is_flush, and it freezes the cache for its whole sweep.

flush_ready gates the counter, so the walk pauses whenever the memory-request queue is near full.
A write-through bank never gates on it — it emits no writebacks at all.
STATE_WAIT2 — every bank EXCEPT bank 0
Banks 1..N−1 wait for bank_empty. Bank 0 skips to
DONE, so its request — the one that propagates the
flush downstream — is the last to be issued.
flush_end — one pulse per bank
STATE_WAIT2: accumulate until
flush_done == {NUM_BANKS{1'b1}}
release ONLY the originating port; its MemReq acks
dcr_flush_if.done — LEVEL-HELD until req drops
DCR response — the flush read finally returns
Core traffic has arbitration PRIORITY
The 2:1 arb puts core_bus_if on input 0, not the
flush. The flush waits until the LSU goes quiet —
which it does, because the host only issues a flush
after busy drops. STICKY hardens the 1-cycle gaps.
Why done is level-held rather than a pulse
One core's flush fans out to the dcache, the icache, and — with graphics enabled — the
socket and cluster gfx caches. Each leg finishes at a different time. Holding every
done high until req drops lets the parent simply AND them together, race-free.
A pulse would need a latch at every junction and would drop legs that finished early.
What the lock buys
Once locked, no core request can reach any bank pipeline. That single fact is what lets
STATE_FLUSH assume the only in-flight entries are its own walk, and it is why WAIT2's
bank_empty check need not re-test mshr_empty — nothing can refill the MSHR.
The cost: the cache is effectively OFF for the whole walk. Every other warp's loads and
stores stall. Flush is linear in cache size and is meant to be infrequent.
Walk length
write-through: LINES_PER_BANK
write-back: LINES_PER_BANK x NUM_WAYS
Write-through clears all ways in parallel (no way_en gate), so one pass over the lines
suffices. Write-back must visit each (way, line) separately because each dirty line
emits its own memory request. All banks walk concurrently.
Reset reuses the same machinery
The FSM's reset state is STATE_INIT, not STATE_IDLE: it walks every line clearing valid
bits, so the tag SRAM needs no async reset — which is what makes it map cleanly to BRAM.
A flush arriving during init is latched and answered immediately: init already invalidated
everything, so the init walk stands in for the flush walk.
